implementation_notes: Rails' custom attribute type is the pattern's Ruby home: one object owns cast (incoming value to Ruby object), serialize (Ruby object to database value) and deserialize (database value to Ruby object) and is attached with attribute :field, MoneyType.new, so the model and the column format never learn about each other. The dependency-free idiom is a Data.define (or Struct) value with to_h plus a self.from_h/self.load pair, or a module with two module functions; a converter class is worth it when one converter serves several models or formats.
code_sketch:
class MoneyType < ActiveModel::Type::Value
  def cast(value) = value.is_a?(Money) ? value : Money.parse(value.to_s)
  def serialize(value) = value.nil? ? nil : "#{value.amount} #{value.currency}"
  def deserialize(value) = value.nil? ? nil : Money.parse(value)
end

class Invoice < ApplicationRecord
  attribute :total, MoneyType.new
end
pitfalls: cast runs on every assignment including form input, so it must raise or return nil deliberately - silently storing junk surfaces later as a corrupted column.
serialize and deserialize receive nil for nullable columns; a type without a nil branch breaks on the first NULL row.
Dirty tracking compares cast values, so the mapped value object needs == and a stable hash or every save marks the attribute changed.
Overriding only deserialize leaves writes on the default cast path, which makes the round trip asymmetric.
